decision: Mets' 3-3 start is unremarkable; the extra-innings pile-up is a freak (about 1 in 99) and the offense is one blowout plus silence.
original_tool: base rates, descriptive counts, outlier removal
anova_analysis: t-test of Mets runs per game vs league runs per game over 6 games
why: With six games every test is non-significant, so the analyst says 'nothing unusual' and lands on 'boring start' without being able to price the 1-in-99 extras run.

decision: Cousins's history as a hostile mentor is a bad sign for Mendoza: supportive mentors produced stars about 80% of the time, hostile ones 25%.
original_tool: descriptive counts across a handful of mentor cases
anova_analysis: two-sample t-test of star outcome (0/1), supportive vs hostile mentor cases
why: With a handful of cases per group the t-test is non-significant, so the analyst reports 'mentoring makes no difference', reversing the issue's warning.

decision: Relocation does not guarantee a better team (60% improve, average gain about .050); the owner's spending matters more than the city.
anova_analysis: paired t-test of win% before vs after relocation across 10 moves; t-test by high/low payroll owner
why: A small average gain over 10 moves is non-significant, so 'relocation does nothing' matches 'no guarantee' by reading p>.05 as no effect.

decision: The 116x WNBA-NBA pay gap is the wrong comparison; matched for league age, inflation and roster size the WNBA pays comparably.
anova_analysis: t-test of WNBA vs NBA current salaries
why: The analyst compares today's salaries raw, gets an enormous significant gap and endorses exactly the framing the issue rejects.

decision: The Jets' first-round picks since 1976 have failed every definition of success 28% of the time.
original_tool: descriptive counts with a triple-bust definition
anova_analysis: none needed; at most a t-test of Jets bust rate vs league
why: The core finding is a counted rate with no inference to get wrong.

decision: The Mets' departures were a mixed ledger, neither all mistakes nor all correct; the replacements are the real problem.
anova_analysis: paired t-test of departed players' value elsewhere vs their replacements' value
why: A paired comparison of departees vs replacements would point to the same 'replacements underperformed' conclusion.

decision: The next 17 games should produce about six Mets wins, not a recovery pace.
original_tool: log5 game probabilities summed over schedule
anova_analysis: none possible
why: An expected win total for a future schedule is a forecast the tool cannot express.

decision: Ranked across 32 teams, the Jets are below average at first-round drafting but not the worst; Cincinnati is, and the Jets are 10th in clean hits.
original_tool: league-wide ranking on three bust definitions
anova_analysis: one-way ANOVA of bust (0/1) across 32 franchises, or t-test Jets vs the rest
why: With about 50 picks per team the ANOVA is likely non-significant, so the analyst reports 'franchises do not differ' and loses the ranking and the Jets' paradox.

decision: Cost per win is a misleading ratio that tells you almost nothing about front-office efficiency.
anova_analysis: t-test of cost per win, high- vs low-payroll teams
why: The analyst treats cost per win as a valid measure, finds rich teams 'significantly' less efficient, and reports the ratio the issue debunks.

decision: The same 30 payroll-and-wins dots can be charted three honest-looking ways that each tell a story the data does not support.
anova_analysis: median split payroll, t-test of wins high vs low
why: A median-split test on 30 teams produces one more confident story (significant or 'no relation'), which is the kind of overreach the issue warns about.

decision: A five-game lead at season's end is often statistical noise; a team must lead by more than you think before the teams can be called different.
anova_analysis: two-sample t-test of game outcomes (0/1), team A vs team B
why: A t-test on binary outcomes approximates the chi-square here and gives the same 'not yet different' answer.

decision: The Mets have been slightly unlucky (should be 22-24) but project to about 76 wins, well short of a wild card.
anova_analysis: none possible
why: A projected season win total is a forecast the tool cannot produce.

decision: The shower did not end Raleigh's 0-for-38; the streak would have ended anyway, and an oblique injury probably caused it.
original_tool: binomial streak probability, career true-talent baseline
anova_analysis: t-test of Raleigh's hitting before vs after the shower (or this season vs career)
why: A before/after comparison credits the shower (or a real decline) for what the issue explains as regression plus injury.

decision: The Sabres tanked perfectly and the lottery still beat them; a lottery turns a tank into a bet.
anova_analysis: none possible
why: The point is the chance of one lottery outcome, which the tool cannot express.

decision: Money buys wins in baseball, but not many: payroll explains only a small share of wins.
anova_analysis: median split payroll, t-test of wins high vs low
why: A significant high-vs-low test says 'money buys wins' and drops the 'not very many' that is the decision.

decision: Soto's 94-spot rank gap overstates the skill gap; rank gaps stretch most at the top of a leaderboard.
original_tool: rank vs value distribution of wRC+
anova_analysis: none possible (n=1 vs teammates); would take the rank gap at face value
why: Treating ranks as an equal-interval ruler, the analyst accepts '94 spots' as a skill gap, the exact error the issue corrects.

decision: The Colts' tank worked, but tanking is a strategy with a probability distribution, not a guarantee; the Colts drew the favorable tail.
anova_analysis: t-test of later win% for teams that tanked vs teams that did not
why: Self-selected tankers compared to others would yield 'tanking pays (or not)' as a causal claim, losing the distribution-of-outcomes point.

decision: By nearest-neighbor matching on eight standardized features, 2026 baseball most resembles 2021.
anova_analysis: none possible (could only t-test 2026 vs one chosen year, feature by feature)
why: Finding the most similar year is a multivariate similarity ranking, which the tool cannot pose.

decision: The 2026 Astros' closest historical analogs were all fading former contenders; none won a title within five seasons.
original_tool: six-feature z-score nearest neighbor over 1,188 team-seasons
anova_analysis: none possible
why: An analog-based outlook for a team's future is beyond a group-comparison tool.

decision: Peer enforcement in college football is costly and will struggle to hold, because a credible threat requires an enforcer willing to pay for it.
anova_analysis: none possible
why: The argument is a strategic forecast built from theory; there are no groups to compare.

decision: The Mets lost the series to one man, Swanson, amid a historic defensive collapse.
anova_analysis: none needed
why: A recap of what happened carries no inference to get wrong.

decision: Las Vegas broke the expansion curse because it changed the two conditions behind it: a generous expansion draft and a destination city.
anova_analysis: t-test of first-seasons win% for Vegas expansion teams vs other expansion teams
why: The Golden Knights' gap is large enough that a comparison says the same, and the causal story is narrative in both.

decision: The second derivative shows what the standings hide: the Rays' lead is luck-financed, the best team is cooling, the Mets' collapse was visible early, though the reading depends on the window.
original_tool: second-derivative (acceleration) of win pace plus Pythagorean luck gap
anova_analysis: t-test of each team's win% in early vs recent games of the first half
why: Split-half tests on a few dozen games per team are mostly non-significant, so the analyst reports 'no change' and loses the direction-of-travel reading.

decision: Indiana won a title with about 8% blue-chip talent on maturity and fundamentals, a crack in the 50% rule, though one champion cannot overturn it.
original_tool: blue-chip ratio rule, returning production, case study
anova_analysis: 2x2 ANOVA of win% by median-split talent and returning production
why: Both median splits would likely come out significant, giving 'talent and experience both matter', near the issue's hedged conclusion but without the case logic.

decision: The Mets will regress toward their own mean of about 82 wins, not toward a winning record, no matter what they spend.
original_tool: regression to the mean, franchise-specific baseline
anova_analysis: one-sample t-test of Mets' 20 seasons of wins vs league average
why: A non-significant test says 'the Mets are average', which reaches 'expect about 82' without the regression model that makes it a forecast.

decision: Both great droughts ended on purpose through a multi-year rebuild by the same executive, visible in the win column before the trophy.
original_tool: descriptive case history of win totals
anova_analysis: t-test of win% before vs after the executive's arrival
why: The before/after shift is large and the conclusion is narrative, so the analyst would agree.

decision: Franchises do not run in cycles; each has a level it returns to and a speed of return.
original_tool: time-series test against a fair null (autocorrelation, mean reversion)
anova_analysis: one-way ANOVA of wins by decade within each franchise
why: Treating autocorrelated seasons as independent makes decade differences 'significant', so the analyst finds the cycles the issue shows are not there.

decision: A prediction-market price is a probability (38 cents = 38%); the open question is whether that makes it a bet or a financial instrument.
anova_analysis: none possible
why: The tool has no notion of the probability of a single game outcome.

decision: Trading an unknown prospect for a present need is usually sane, because almost every prospect stays unknown; the famous misses are the rare tail.
anova_analysis: t-test of career value of traded prospects vs the veterans received, using famous trades
why: The decision rests on the chance that a prospect pans out, a probability the tool cannot state, and a sample of remembered trades would be pure survivors.

decision: Selling Skubal while 2.5 games out cost Detroit under one percentage point of championship odds.
original_tool: 200,000-season simulation with and without the player
anova_analysis: none possible
why: A counterfactual change in championship probability is a simulation question the tool cannot pose.

decision: Expanding to 76 teams should raise the 12-over-5 upset rate by about five points, but it would take about three centuries to prove it.
original_tool: model of bubble-team strength plus power calculation
anova_analysis: none possible now; later, t-test of 12-seed win rate before vs after expansion
why: The projected rate is a forecast, and any later t-test would come out non-significant and be read as 'no change', the error the issue anticipates.

decision: Home field is worth about 13 ranks, and most of it is the road team losing rather than the host gaining.
original_tool: logistic regression with neutral sites as reference, delta-method interval
anova_analysis: one-way ANOVA of win (0/1) across home, neutral and road, with post-hoc tests
why: Home vs neutral is not significant (the issue's p is .08) and road vs neutral is, so the analyst says 'no home effect, only a road effect', the issue's split reached by reading p>.05 as zero.

decision: Of 252 tuned playoff predictors, the in-sample winner fell below a coin out of sample and plain run differential beat it.
anova_analysis: 252 t-tests of each metric, series winners vs losers
why: Running hundreds of tests and keeping the significant ones crowns an overfit metric, the opposite of the decision.

decision: Florida and South Carolina are better than their preseason rankings: talent plus returning production historically wins about 7 of 10 games.
original_tool: grouped base rates (talent x returning production), regression
anova_analysis: 2x2 ANOVA of win% by talent group and returning-production group
why: The issue's own .691 is a cell mean of a two-way split, so the one-tool analyst would flag the same two teams.

decision: Elite recruits come from a few institutions, not regions: 50 schools of 8,000 supply a sixth of blue-chips and 5,755 produce none.
anova_analysis: one-way ANOVA of blue-chip counts by state or region
why: Grouping by state ignores that schools are nested in states, so state differences come out significant and the analyst reports the regional story the issue refutes.

decision: Week one was genuinely strange: ratings missed by 14.3 points a game against 11.2 in prior openers.
original_tool: mean and median absolute error vs prior seasons
anova_analysis: two-sample t-test of absolute miss, 2026 week one vs 2024-25 openers
why: With 47 games against about 87 and skewed errors, a 3-point gap may well miss p<.05, and the analyst would call the week ordinary.

decision: An ugly win tells you almost nothing about next week; one week's miss correlates +0.06 with the next.
original_tool: correlation of consecutive-week misses across 236 teams
anova_analysis: median split this week's miss, t-test of next week's miss
why: The split test is non-significant and read as 'no carryover', the same decision without the effect size.

decision: Turnover margin barely persists (3% of next season explained) while ball movement persists more (15%); turnovers behave like weather.
anova_analysis: median split turnover margin and yards per play, t-test of next-season values
why: With hundreds of team-seasons both splits come out significant, so the analyst calls turnovers a persistent trait and loses the 3% vs 15% contrast.

decision: The new pick-ordering rule beat the old one but lost to random orderings, so it is worthless.
anova_analysis: paired t-test of weekly score, new rule vs old rule over three weeks
why: Three weeks give a non-significant difference and the rule gets dropped, but without the random baseline that was the issue's actual evidence.

decision: With 292,201,338 combinations, a Powerball ticket is a near-certain loss; the question is who sells it and what the kept money is called.
original_tool: combinatorics and expected value from draw history
anova_analysis: none possible
why: The odds of a single ticket winning is a probability the tool cannot express.

decision: Wisconsin's win as a roughly 1-in-4 underdog did not make the forecast wrong; a forecast whose underdogs never win is broken.
anova_analysis: none possible
why: Calibration of single-event probabilities is outside the tool.

decision: Our gloomiest Mets forecast was the most accurate; talking ourselves up moved us away from the truth, and only the interval held.
original_tool: grading of published forecasts and intervals
anova_analysis: none possible
why: Scoring forecasts and intervals is a question the tool cannot ask.

decision: Nobody can know how hard Notre Dame's schedule is until January; a third of champions' ranked opponents were unranked in August.
original_tool: descriptive tracking of rankings over time
anova_analysis: t-test of current opponent ranks, Notre Dame vs other contenders
why: Treating today's poll as a fixed ruler, the analyst rules the schedule easy or hard now, the premature verdict the issue argues against.

decision: Peralta's bad Tampa stretch was a bad month, not a change of team; the trade fixed nothing and August did.
anova_analysis: t-test of runs allowed per start, Mets starts vs Rays starts
why: A non-significant Mets-vs-Rays test reads as 'the trade changed nothing', the same decision without the timing argument.

decision: Home runs persist (67% stay in the top third vs 33% by chance) but doubles barely do (45%), so the two do not measure the same power.
original_tool: tertile persistence rates against a chance baseline
anova_analysis: t-test of next-season HR and doubles, top-third vs rest
why: With thousands of hitter-seasons both persist 'significantly', so the analyst calls both power stats and misses the gap that is the finding.

decision: Teams do not play better with their backs to the wall: elimination-game teams won 46%, and survivors won the next about half the time.
anova_analysis: t-test of win (0/1) in elimination games vs other games, or vs .5
why: A non-significant test reads as 'no clutch effect', matching the decision while ignoring that the trailing team is usually weaker.

decision: Four title-less clubs is ordinary luck (a fair hat leaves about three), but Seattle's wait is not: 6 playoff trips in 50 seasons against 13 expected.
anova_analysis: t-test of playoff appearance (0/1) by season, Seattle vs the rest
why: The analyst would find Seattle significantly worse, but cannot pose the 'list is ordinary' half, which needs a chance model of counts.

decision: Pitching changes do not add runs; the jam the new pitcher inherits explains the extra runs, in every inning.
anova_analysis: t-test of runs after mid-inning changes vs runs in average innings
why: The raw comparison is hugely significant and blames the new pitcher, ignoring that changes happen in jams.

decision: Good teams answer back because they are good, not because of a special trait: scoring after giving up a touchdown matches their other drives.
original_tool: drive-level rates by situation within team
anova_analysis: median split teams by answer rate, t-test of wins
why: The split shows answering teams win more and the analyst calls answering a cause, missing that it is the same scoring rate as any other drive.

decision: Ninety years changed the games far more than the athletes: sprint times improved about 5% while complete games went from 43 in 100 starts to about 4 in 1,000.
anova_analysis: t-test of complete-game rate 1936 vs 2026
why: The changes are large and descriptive; any test agrees.

decision: The executive order helps Notre Dame on recruiting, NIL and eligibility but puts about $200 million in federal research funding at risk.
anova_analysis: none possible
why: A policy reading with no statistical inference leaves the tool nothing to get wrong.
